name: Defense and Mil-Spec Work
scope: ITAR realities, paperwork-as-engineering, decade-scale projects, qualification culture

claims.claim_text: Military contracts commonly require a supplier to support a product for ten to fifteen years, which forces the designer to obtain written statements from component vendors committing to supply the part over that horizon. Such statements are difficult to extract and are the reason a secondary industry in obsolete-part supply exists.
claims.quote_verbatim: have to guarantee 10, 15 year, uh, lifespans on, on actually supporting these products. So you've actually got to try and get written, um, uh, you know, statements from the suppliers saying, yes, we, we will still support this chip in 10 or 15 years time. And it's like extracting teeth
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: What's In A Name?

claims.claim_text: Obsolete-part specialists such as Rochester Electronics operate their own wafer fab and approach the original chip designer when a part is going obsolete, buying the mask set rather than the schematics so that the vendor's IP concerns are avoided.
claims.quote_verbatim: Rochester actually has a wafer fab. The way that those guys work is they buy when a chip is going obsolete. They approach the original designer of the chip and say, hey, can we buy? We don't need the schematics of the chip because we know that there's IP involved or whatever. Yeah. They just want the mask
claims.speaker: Vincent Himpe
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Vincent Himpe - Escaped Electron Elocution

claims.claim_text: Obsolete-part re-manufacturers select which chips to keep alive by end market, concentrating on parts saleable to military customers, so a commercial designer whose part is discontinued cannot assume the aftermarket will cover it.
claims.quote_verbatim: Rochester is only interested in chips that they can sell to the military
claims.speaker: Vincent Himpe
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Vincent Himpe - Escaped Electron Elocution

claims.claim_text: In military programmes HDL is classified as source code and therefore falls under software verification rules requiring every line to be verified, at a rule-of-thumb cost of around one hundred dollars per line. Design teams avoided the rule by entering FPGA designs as schematic capture instead of HDL.
claims.quote_verbatim: They used schematic capture instead of HDL because if it was HDL, it was deemed to be source code. So source code came under a different set of rules which meant that they had to verify each line of code in their product, right? And, you know, it would cost like, you know, there's some generic cost of like $100 per line of code to, you know, verify code in the military world
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Dave Vandenbout - Xceptional XESS Xenagogue

claims.claim_text: On defence programmes the specification is not negotiable and cost is not a design variable; the engineer's obligation is to meet the stated performance whatever the bill of materials costs.
claims.quote_verbatim: job is to meet the specs regardless of cost, you know? You have to meet that performance
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Design Reviews Are Important - Habitual Hype Hebetude

claims.claim_text: Engineers moving from defence work to consumer or high-volume work have to acquire per-unit cost discipline they never needed, because military design optimises for performance alone and not for component cost.
claims.quote_verbatim: military stuff, it was, you know, you didn't care about component cost. Right. It's about performance only
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Inspirations and Aspirations - Recanting Rocket Rationale

claims.claim_text: A defence product development cycle runs on the order of five years, after which the design is frozen and manufactured essentially unchanged for twenty years; industrial products by comparison run eighteen to twenty-four month cycles.
claims.quote_verbatim: five years. It is finished, and you're going to be able to make it for 20 years
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Is This A Show?

claims.claim_text: Where a customer demands five to ten years of product support, parts with uncertain supply lifetimes are simply unavailable to the designer regardless of their technical merit.
claims.quote_verbatim: customers demand five, 10-year product support times. There is no chance in hell I could ever choose a part like this
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: The Cost Of Doing Business

claims.claim_text: Defence and medical device work impose comparable regulatory burdens, and the burden extends to test engineering as much as to design.
claims.quote_verbatim: medical industry is just like the military industry I've worked in, very regulated, highly regulated
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Call In Show #3

claims.claim_text: In heavily regulated defence and medical programmes the qualification and documentation load can make selecting a single mechanical fastener a six-month exercise.
claims.quote_verbatim: spend six months choosing and selecting the right screw. You know, like, I'm not kidding. You know, it's like – it can be that anal
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Call In Show #3

claims.claim_text: Component brokers who accumulate stock and resell it at multiples of the original price are viable because military and aerospace buyers can absorb those prices; commercial and hobbyist buyers are not the intended customer for that channel.
claims.quote_verbatim: we are not the customers for that it is the military is the customer for that and aerospace and that is so it's fine if that model extends to industrial and maybe commercial like this which is seems like it might but yeah the i can never i will never and can never pay aerospace or uh military prices
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Stefan Dzisiewski-Smith

claims.claim_text: A contractual ten to twenty year service life makes part selection a compliance decision rather than an engineering one: a designer is not permitted to specify a component whose supply cannot be guaranteed across that period.
claims.quote_verbatim: they had to have by contract, like a 10, 20 year service life. Right. We, I would not, as a designer, I was not allowed to use a chip like this
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: World Trade Futurity (WTF)

claims.claim_text: Equipment for industrial and military racks is still built to be repaired and serviced, because enclosure volume is not a binding constraint in rack-mounted applications and space can be spent on serviceability.
claims.quote_verbatim: they still do in some like big in, in industrial and other markets. They do make, and military as we'll get into. Sure. They, you know, make things repairable still and they make them, you know, because like space really isn't like a real huge issue for those, you know, for things that go inside racks and, you know, stuff like that, like size isn't really a big deal. Right. So you can often make things serviceable
claims.episode_title: Bill and Dave's Excellent Equipment

claims.claim_text: Connector prices of around two hundred US dollars per unit are routine in defence electronics.
claims.quote_verbatim: $200 us connectors are the norm. Right. Oh yeah. Each per unit
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: The Almighty Dollarydoo

claims.claim_text: A connector specified by a military customer can be sole-sourced to a single manufacturer at around nine hundred dollars a unit, and being sole-sourced does not guarantee quality.
claims.quote_verbatim: the connector was $900. Yeah. It was like a specced by the Navy, you know, like, you know, the only one company made them
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: The Almighty Dollarydoo

claims.claim_text: As recently as the early to mid 2000s, large defence contractors maintained design documentation on numbered A3 graph sheets, with computer-drawn circuits printed out and glued onto the sheets, because the controlled record was the paper sheet rather than the CAD file.
claims.quote_verbatim: everything was done on these A3 size graph sheets. Right. Hand, hand drawn on these A, you know, and you would stick things in
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Hipster Fodder

claims.claim_text: Programmable logic retains a substantial defence market, and defence customers form a sizeable part of the business of smaller FPGA vendors.
claims.quote_verbatim: programmable logic in general has a lot of use cases in automotive, in military. We've got a big business in, in middle of our defense customers that like to use programmable logic
claims.speaker: Brian Faith
claims.episode_title: Open FPGA Toolchains and Machine Learning with Brian Faith of QuickLogic

claims.claim_text: Consolidation among qualified defence board houses interacts badly with procurement rules: when only about three shops can meet the requirements but every job must attract two or three bids, the same work is repeatedly bid to the same suppliers and price competition disappears.
claims.quote_verbatim: there's fewer and fewer board houses that can do this sort of thing. And then there's more and more, you know, they're going to layer on top of that all of the shortages and all the requirements. And it's like, oh, my God. Like, they're down to, like, three houses. They mandatorily have to get, like, two or three bids for every job. Yeah, yeah. And so now they keep bidding the same stuff to the same people
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: The Rodeo Drive of Electronics

claims.claim_text: Obsolete-part houses sell long-term sourcing service contracts, undertaking to supply a part for ten years to customers such as government and defence programmes whose original vendor will not commit to that horizon.
claims.quote_verbatim: Rochester basically buys up old wafers. They then have like service contracts for people who say, I need, I need this to source for 10 years. The vendor can do it. For the military, for the government, that sort of thing
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: The Rodeo Drive of Electronics

claims.claim_text: Sorting a distributor catalogue by descending price surfaces military parts at the top; the most expensive single chip found in such a search was around $128,000.
claims.quote_verbatim: You want to see some military parts. You will find some military parts. Yes. And that's exactly what I found. Right. And the most expensive chip was $22,000. No, no. It was a hundred and a hundred, no, $128,000
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: The Rodeo Drive of Electronics

claims.claim_text: A large share of US defence assembly is done by small family-run shops whose owners are retiring without successors, leaving no replacement capacity for the specific parts they have been making for decades.
claims.quote_verbatim: So much military stuff in the US at least is like these mom and pop assembly shops. They've been making a lot of the same stuff, you know, for better or worse, right? It's been like their livelihood and they're all retiring and they're, you know, their kids, their kids went off to other places or in software or whatever. They're, you know, there's just no backfill
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Psst...Hey buddy, wanna buy an Octopus?

claims.claim_text: Onshoring a defence supply chain fails when the sole historic supplier of a part has already gone out of business, because the capability cannot be recreated by placing an order.
claims.quote_verbatim: there was only one company that made this stuff and now they're out of business because you didn't keep them in business
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Psst...Hey buddy, wanna buy an Octopus?

claims.claim_text: Very expensive military signal-processing parts are justified by workloads such as adaptive-bandwidth phased-array radar, which requires processing on the order of a thousand simultaneous channels at one gigasample per second in real time.
claims.quote_verbatim: a thousand simultaneous channels at one gig sample per second all in real-time, you know, for your adaptive bandwidth phased array bloody radar
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Tugging on the Nerd Heartstring

claims.claim_text: Defence contractors sometimes remark every integrated circuit on a board with their own part numbers, so the underlying devices cannot be identified from the assembly.
claims.quote_verbatim: he had some old military board where every chip got rebadged. So he didn't know what any of the guts were, but you know, they were all badged by the defense company
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Tektronix, ChipReport.tv, & the Signal Path - Temperative Tegmen Temperature

claims.claim_text: MIT Lincoln Laboratory works primarily on US military programmes together with FAA and NASA work, on a budget approaching a billion dollars a year and with well over three thousand employees.
claims.quote_verbatim: They work on primarily government, military things, and FAA and NASA stuff, but mostly for the military, the U.S. military. Mm-hmm. And it's... I think the budget is something on the order of not quite a billion, but close, last I recall. A billion. Before I left. And I think that they were well over 3,000 employees
claims.speaker: Greg Charvat
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Dr Greg Charvat - Watcher of Wraithlike Walls

claims.claim_text: A public portfolio of personal projects, generally an asset when job hunting, can count against a candidate seeking classified defence work; open-source work can be shown but a fully public record of everything is a liability.
claims.quote_verbatim: if you really want to work on like high tech military stuff, sometimes that is dicey. I mean, you could show your past stuff. It was like open source projects and stuff like that, but yeah, you don't necessarily want to show everything or, you know, live your life completely open
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Google Glass, Lean Startup and VotC - Initializing Instructed Interviews

claims.claim_text: Specialist manufacturers keep long-obsolete processors in production for defence and space programmes, producing runs as small as ten units at prices on the order of ten thousand dollars per chip.
claims.quote_verbatim: They will actually still make the, you know, the 888 processor or something because it's used in some, you know, space shuttle or something like that. Right, right. And there's a market for another 10 of them. So, they will actually produce them at, you know, $10,000 a chip
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Military Electronics and The Free Eagle (Freagle) Campaign

claims.claim_text: Underwater military sonar equipment used high-energy lithium batteries carrying enough stored energy to explode on a short circuit, and shipping those assemblies required substantial dangerous-goods paperwork.
claims.quote_verbatim: I used to work on a project for the military. It was a underwater. Sonos is, we had these huge high energy lithium batteries in it. And yeah, I know the paperwork that goes into trying to get those things shipped and woof, boy, you know, like if these things shorted out, they would blow up
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: DJ and Jazzy Jeff

claims.claim_text: Marine and underwater equipment, both military and civil, historically had no EMC or emissions standard to design to outside territorial waters, and the industry had no in-house standards either; the only acceptance test was whether the equipment did its job.
claims.quote_verbatim: I never had to design to EMC. The only rule is there are no rules. Anything. And yeah, so all the, so all the military, all, all the marine underwater military stuff I worked on, all the, um, all the civil stuff I worked on for the underwater seismic stuff and, and boat based stuff as well. Equipment goes on. None of that had to meet any standards at all
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Ludicrously High Frequency Interference

claims.claim_text: Defence programmes routinely build a total quantity of one unit, which removes the usual economic basis for cost optimisation, though a designer would still not specify a thousand-dollar part where a hundred-dollar part would do.
claims.quote_verbatim: I've worked in the military side of things where sometimes you'll make one of something, you know, a grand total of one
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: OSHW, Makerbot & Memristo - Maundering Memristor Mathematicaster

claims.claim_text: Fielded military electronics lagged commercial technology by roughly twenty years around 2000 and by only five to ten years two decades later, meaning defence deployment cycles accelerated faster than the commercial industry over that period.
claims.quote_verbatim: go back to year 2000, at that point, the military was maybe 20 years behind in terms of electronics technology deployed in the field. Compared to commercial applications. And you look at now, and maybe they're only five or 10 years behind
claims.speaker: Howard Johnson
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Dr. Howard Johnson - Winsome Waveform Wizardry

claims.claim_text: Military hardware is typically about ten years behind current technology by the time it is fielded, so a maintenance cycle ten years later requires sourcing twenty-year-old chips, sustaining a niche market in recovered die and legacy parts.
claims.quote_verbatim: A lot of military stuff is, you know, I mean, it's already 10 years behind when it actually gets released. And then 10 years later, when you've got to maintain it again, you're using 20-year-old chips. So you've got to go out and find that 20-year-old processor
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Otiose Ontocyclic Opiniasters

claims.claim_text: Obsolete processors such as the 6502 survive in defence equipment because maintaining a legacy design costs less than requalifying a redesign, not because the part is technically preferred.
claims.quote_verbatim: There'd be a few massively legacy designs in the military or something somewhere, you know, some old bit of gear, which, you know, it's just easier to maintain it than it is to redesign it from scratch
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Jersey Jeff Jactitation

claims.claim_text: The 5400 logic series released in 1964 was a military-grade part, and the commercial 7400 series followed roughly two years later; the first IC-based project to appear in hobbyist magazines dates to 1967.
claims.quote_verbatim: that was only the 5400 stuff for the military project. So it's not surprising that you wouldn't find it in the hobbyist and commercial mags
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: B Plus Boards and D Minus Cities - Uneath Urban Ubication

claims.claim_text: Export control regimes such as ITAR are enforced at the point of transaction: semiconductor vendors gate software downloads and parts orders behind end-use declarations that the buyer must affirm.
claims.quote_verbatim: the reason this list exists is the same reason that there's like ITAR when you have to like check boxes for like – I know that when you download software from TI, they always make you check big boxes
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Someone is watching...we think - Horme Hostility Hypochondriac

claims.claim_text: Export-controlled products cannot be sold into certain countries, with the controlled list weighted toward items with nuclear proliferation relevance; liability for a false end-use declaration falls on the party who ticked the box.
claims.quote_verbatim: it's usually something to do with nuclear proliferation type stuff. But it's like you can't sell to certain countries and because – I don't know all the rules, but I do know that if you – if basically if they trace it back to you through – and then you would check that box, at that point you're in deep doo-doo kind of thing
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Someone is watching...we think - Horme Hostility Hypochondriac

claims.claim_text: US export control reaches transactions with no US party: a buyer was flagged on a US government watch list for purchasing non-US parts from a UK company out of stock already held in Australia.
claims.quote_verbatim: They're not US parts. Okay. No. And I get flagged by a US. I get flagged on a US government watch list. Because a UK company is selling parts to an Australian in Australia that are already stocked in Australia
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Someone is watching...we think - Horme Hostility Hypochondriac

claims.claim_text: US defence customers dropped an EDA vendor after it moved research and development to China, because US regulations restrict which products a defence contractor may buy from a company effectively based there. Where engineering work is performed is therefore a market-access decision, not only a cost decision.
claims.quote_verbatim: Altium, are now starting to lose a lot of business, a lot of their military contracts, U.S. military companies, who did not like the fact that they were in China. Oh, interesting. You know, doing their R&D in China, because apparently there are rules and regulations in the U.S. about how you can deal and what products you can get from a company that is effectively based in China
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Spacing Out On Space - Dave's Dongle Designing

claims.claim_text: Ordinary catalogue components can carry export control obligations: a forty-dollar thermal sensor array could not be bought from a distributor without first signing an export control agreement, and two attempts to order it failed.
claims.quote_verbatim: I failed twice at getting this chip because you have to sign an export control agreement
claims.speaker: Noah Feehan
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Noah Feehan - Biloquistic Blinking Blush

claims.claim_text: Export-controlled parts propagate the compliance burden to anyone reselling a board that contains them, which is enough on its own to stop a small designer from offering an otherwise open design for sale.
claims.quote_verbatim: I don't have the time or professional inclination to deal with export control for my end users
claims.speaker: Noah Feehan
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Noah Feehan - Biloquistic Blinking Blush

claims.claim_text: Silicon for US government customers must come from a certified domestic process and cannot leave the country, which rules out offshore foundries irrespective of cost or capability.
claims.quote_verbatim: it's a certified process in the U.S. So, if you make stuff for the government, for government customers, and it cannot leave the country. So, it has to be manufactured in the United States
claims.speaker: Shahriar Shahramian
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Shahriar from The Signal Path - Quisquous Quivering Quadripole

claims.claim_text: Software-defined radio hardware sold at retail can carry export control restrictions that delay shipment outside the United States.
claims.quote_verbatim: This product has some level of export control restriction. So, expect delay when shipping outside of the US
claims.episode_title: A Security Update with Michael Ossmann

claims.claim_text: Radio hardware faces import restrictions as well as export restrictions; a shipment can clear the seller's export rules and still be blocked by the destination government.
claims.quote_verbatim: It certainly is a problem in many countries. Right. For example, I just got an email from SparkFun today about somebody, about a customer who's trying to buy one of these from India. And the Indian government doesn't want to let it in
claims.episode_title: A Security Update with Michael Ossmann

claims.claim_text: Sanctions imposed after the invasion of Ukraine barred Russia and Belarus from buying Taiwanese CPUs rated above 25 MHz, a threshold set on clock rate rather than on part category.
claims.quote_verbatim: Who now cannot buy any CPU From Taiwan Over 25 meg
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: AI aren't sentient yet...right?

claims.claim_text: Export restrictions on advanced compute hardware to China apply to specified performance levels of a vendor's range rather than to the vendor's whole product line.
claims.quote_verbatim: there's China's kind of getting cut off from certain stuff. So like apparently they're not allowed to have NVIDIA stuff anymore. Yep. And there's been some. Well, a certain NVIDIA stuff, not all NVIDIA. It's not. No. Certain levels
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Rigorous engineering stuff may be out the window

claims.claim_text: Performance-threshold export control is long-established: a PlayStation console was export controlled because its GPU crossed a supercomputing threshold that made it usable for simulating weapon implosions.
claims.quote_verbatim: it was one of the PlayStations was such a supercomputer level at the time that there were export controls. You could not sell it to uranium fancy in countries. Let's put it that way. Who might build some gadget? Because they could use this for simulating, you know, implosions of certain devices
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Rigorous engineering stuff may be out the window

claims.claim_text: China imposed export controls on germanium and gallium, both inputs with no immediate drop-in substitute for compound-semiconductor and optoelectronic supply chains.
claims.quote_verbatim: china stopped exporting uh there's a germanium it was germanium and it was something else uh gallium
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: For a couple weeks there...

claims.claim_text: China accounted for roughly 60 percent of world germanium output and about 80 percent of gallium output at the time export controls on those materials were announced.
claims.quote_verbatim: it says 60 germanium 80 of gallium
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: For a couple weeks there...

claims.claim_text: Space systems classified as defence dual-use force the entire manufacturing chain in-country: neither bills of materials nor circuit assemblies can be sent overseas without an export control approval, so design, layout and assembly are all kept local.
claims.quote_verbatim: because our space systems are listed as defense dual use, all of our manufacturing is done in Australia. So we can't actually send any of our bills, materials or circuit assemblies overseas without export control
claims.speaker: Dan Esparon
claims.episode_title: Satellite Design Engineering with Dan Esparon

claims.claim_text: US Atomic Energy Commission funding of technology development came with a sales restriction limiting the resulting products to American buyers, an early instance of state funding carrying export conditions.
claims.quote_verbatim: we'll cut you a check for $30 million and you can sell them. But you can only sell them to other Americans
claims.speaker: Kent Lundberg
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Dr. Kent Lundberg - Luculent Linear Legacy

claims.claim_text: High-bandwidth oscilloscopes and low-current instrumentation carried export restrictions because, until the mid to late 1990s, the applications needing that performance were nuclear instrumentation; the restrictions persisted after commercial communications work moved into the same frequency range.
claims.quote_verbatim: the reason you'd want a really fast scope is because you were looking at neutrons or something. Well, they, they had the same restrictions as a Keithley, but they still have them. I mean, basically they still, they're still all export restricted
claims.speaker: Kent Lundberg
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Dr. Kent Lundberg - Luculent Linear Legacy

claims.claim_text: The MIT Radiation Laboratory series, the standard reference collection on radar circuits, antennas, klystrons and microwave instrumentation, was itself export restricted.
claims.quote_verbatim: you can't actually read these books because they're export restricted
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Dr. Kent Lundberg - Luculent Linear Legacy

claims.claim_text: Distributors require an end-use declaration before an order can be completed, asking whether the parts will be used in military, government surveillance, nuclear or chemical weapons applications, regardless of how ordinary the parts are.
claims.quote_verbatim: before you can finish your shopping cart and buy them, you have to fill out this little thing which, you know, says, are these products going to be used in military things? Are they going to be used for government surveillance? Are they going to be used in nuclear bloody weapons and chemical weapons and all that sort of stuff
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Love Robots and Pantyhose Screens

claims.claim_text: A declaration of personal use can trigger follow-up questioning from the distributor demanding further project detail, even on an order consisting only of LEDs, resistors and op-amps.
claims.quote_verbatim: I get an email from DigiKey saying, oh, we need more details on your project. What exactly are these parts going to be used in
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Love Robots and Pantyhose Screens

claims.claim_text: Written ten-year supply assurances can eventually be obtained from component vendors for defence designs, but they are difficult to get and are not reliable, since a vendor's commitment can be withdrawn or misstated later.
claims.quote_verbatim: got to get written assurances from the companies to ensure that they're going to supply that part for the next 10 years. Because if I'm designing something for the military, they require like a 10 plus year lifetime. And you've got to get assurance that they will supply that part in 10 years. And it's very difficult to get
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Love Robots and Pantyhose Screens

claims.claim_text: Because vendor supply assurances cannot be fully trusted, long-life designs are protected by specifying second-source parts or parts whose family shares a common footprint, so a substitute can be dropped in without a board respin.
claims.quote_verbatim: use second source parts or use parts with a common footprint in their family
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Love Robots and Pantyhose Screens
